status_reason: A decision on patients during live surgery needs validation beyond a first assessment, and the kidney study cannot be quoted as readiness proof; the study's own authors state much work remains and false negatives are unacceptable.
answer: No, the kidney study cannot be quoted as proof that the sensor is ready for live tumour-boundary decisions. It is an in vitro proof of concept on 14 thawed samples from 7 patients, and the surgical scenario is an application concept without validation data. The next step is a laboratory study on kidney tissue with independent histology, followed by new in vivo data.

inline.headline: Test NIR diffuse reflectance on kidney tumour and normal tissue in the lab before any surgical use
inline.probe: NIR diffuse reflectance probe for scattering samples, 0.5 to 1 mm
inline.install: first on excised tissue in the laboratory; in the surgical field only after validation
inline.test_against: combined MIR ATR and fluorescence probe on the same spot
inline.not_final_because: Only thawed ex vivo samples exist so far, spectra can differ in vivo, NIR penetrates about 3 mm, the 2500 nm upper NIR limit exceeds the 2400 nm fiber range, and no data exist on the client's own setup.

problems.text: The kidney study is not proof of surgical readiness: it tested two prototypes on 14 in vitro samples from 7 patients, the authors call it a proof of concept with very high variance in cancer tissue and unacceptable false negatives, and much work remains.

The live-surgery use is an application concept on a multispectral laboratory set-up with no validation data; the study can only be quoted as an in vitro proof of concept that an LED NIR sensor captured tumour-related variance in kidney samples.
The samples were thawed frozen biopsies measured ex vivo, and their spectra can differ from real in vivo measurements, so new in vivo data are needed.
Only four LEDs were used; the LED set and wavelengths must be adapted to each organ and tumour type, so a different sensor or organ needs new data.

methods.why: NIR is the most common online fiber-probe method and penetrates several millimetres, and the study's LED set used 900 to 1500 nm, so it is the client's concept to test first.
Combined NIR and IR gave benefits for tumour boundaries, and ATR probes suit liquids and elastic solids, so it is the first alternative to compare.
A broad fluorescence band at 520 to 530 nm from FAD is formed in tissue, and combined fluorescence and ATR IR detected the tumour boundary in model tissue.
Raman carries information complementary to MIR but its signals are weak and can be masked by fluorescence in many organic samples.

questions.q: Will the sensor measure fresh tissue in vivo, or thawed ex vivo samples?
questions.why: The current study used thawed frozen biopsies, and their spectra can differ from in vivo.

questions.q: What exact decision will the sensor support (tumour yes or no, or margin distance), and what false-negative rate is acceptable?
questions.why: False negatives are unacceptable in oncology, so the accuracy target defines the test.

questions.q: How many patients, samples and organs are planned, and will each organ use its own LED or wavelength set?
questions.why: The study covered 14 samples from 7 patients in one organ, and the LED set must be adapted per case.

questions.q: How will the probe reach the tissue during surgery, with contact or at a distance?
questions.why: Probe contact and distance change the diffuse reflectance signal, and NIR penetrates only about 3 mm.

experiment.objective: Test whether NIR, with MIR ATR and fluorescence as comparators, separates kidney tumour from normal tissue against independent histology.
steps: Collect matched tumour and normal kidney samples with independent histological reference of tumour discrimination.
Measure NIR spectra with the client's probe over the planned range using a fiber covering it (350 to 2400 nm).
Measure MIR ATR and fluorescence on the same spots where samples are suitable for ATR.
Validate with segmented cross-validation and randomisation tests, and compare each method against the best single method on the same validation data.
Repeat with new in vivo or matched live-condition data before any surgical claim.
references: S03 p.14 (segmented CV and randomisation tests)
experiment.go_no_go: Criteria come from the client; none were stated in the enquiry.

pathway.key_features: Not yet known; to be identified from the laboratory spectra by multivariate analysis, with the NIR LED wavelengths as the starting point.
pathway.path_reason: The client needs multi-method laboratory validation before a chemometric model or custom system can be selected.

multispectral.why: MIR gives the fat and protein amide fingerprint bands, and fluorescence gives FAD emission, so the information is complementary; in model tissue neither method alone separated all classes, but the fused data did.
multispectral.test: Measure both methods on the same kidney spots and compare the fused model with the best single method on the same validation data; the combination counts only if it wins.

assumptions: The client's sensor is a similar LED NIR design to the study, since its design is not stated.
